limits: Verified never means interoperability with a device the design talks to unless a board measurement against that device is listed in the record; a design that checks its own output against its own model accepts its own symmetric mistakes.

Verified never means timing beyond the stated corner: a post-route timing result is for the part, speed grade, clock and tool version in its evidence file, not for other corners, temperatures or devices.

Verified never means beyond the widths and depths checked: a simulation covers the vectors it ran, a bounded formal result covers the stated depth only, and a per-width proof covers the widths it names; only a Lean proof marked all widths covers every width, and only for its model.

Verified never means the requirement is the right one: the text of a requirement is the human's check (or the planner's, where the record says delegated), and a record shows that checks exist and pass, not that nothing was left out.
Verified never means a hardware or board result unless a board measurement item is listed; a simulation is not the board.
Verified is about the files in the manifest at the hashes given. A change to any of them makes the record out of date (the CI check fails), and the evidence stale until it is re-recorded.
An agreement or acceptance recorded as delegated is the planner's decision on the owner's delegation, not a human sign-off; the record counts it apart.
2 requirements depend on an element outside the design and have not been closed by hardware, so they hold in simulation only: B119-F-MACPAIR, B119-F-REALPEER.

7 performance requirements are verified in simulation only, not measured on the board: B119-P-FIRSTBYTE, B119-P-IPCKSUM, B119-P-TCPCKSUM, B119-P-SEGMENT, B119-P-RATE, B119-P-TOP-SPEC, B119-P-TOP-VERDICT.
3 performance requirements are verified by post-route timing at one corner: B119-P-TIMING, B119-P-HOLD, B119-P-AREA.
Lean proofs here are of a transcription of the RTL, not of the RTL itself: B119-F-CKSUM-IP, B119-F-CKSUM-TCP, B119-F-CKSUM-MODEL.

item_views.title: IPv4 header checksum equals the Internet checksum
The filled-in header sums to 0xFFFF (receiver check)

requirements.text: Brief 119's tcp_fast.sv builds the IPv4 header checksum from a precomputed template plus the changing fields. For all TTL, address and identification values it equals the complement of the ones' complement sum of the header, and the filled-in header sums to 0xFFFF.
requirements.title: The IPv4 header checksum of the TCP fast path equals the Internet checksum, for all inputs

item_views.title: TCP checksum equals the Internet checksum, payloads up to 30 words

requirements.text: For all addresses, ports, sequence and acknowledgement numbers, windows and payloads of up to 30 sixteen-bit words, the checksum the RTL equations produce equals the complement of the ones' complement sum over pseudo-header, header and payload. The byte-pair swapping, the streaming receive check and the timing are not modelled.
requirements.title: The TCP checksum of the TCP fast path equals the Internet checksum, for all inputs and payloads up to 30 words

item_views.title: Ones complement sum equals the natural-number sum mod 65535
RFC 1624 equation 3 is correct for headers of any length
The all-zero header corner gives 0x0000

requirements.text: The ones' complement sum of any list of 16-bit words equals the natural-number sum reduced mod 65535, and RFC 1624 equation 3 (incremental update) is correct for a header of any length when the new header is not all zero words; for an all-zero header it gives 0x0000. No current RTL patches a checksum in place; this is the arithmetic the fast path's template-plus-fields form relies on.
requirements.title: The ones' complement arithmetic the checksum equations rest on is correct, for lists of any length
